opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a particular kind of knowledge you only get from actually carrying something all the way through. In science, it's really easy to work on a piece of a problem: you optimize one assay, or you build one tool, or you run one analysis, and you can feel very productive. But when you take a project from the initial idea, through figuring out whether it's even the right question, through building the methods, debugging all the things that break, getting to a result, and then actually communicating it and getting it out into the world, you learn where the real bottlenecks are. And they're almost never where you expected them to be at the start.

For me, a lot of that came from early experiences in the lab, especially working on genome editing, where you'd have this beautiful concept, and then the reality was months of figuring out delivery, or specificity, or just why the cells weren't happy. Going end to end teaches you taste. You develop an intuition for which problems are tractable, which ones are going to eat two years of your life, and which corners you can cut versus which ones will come back to bite you.

It also changes how you lead. When you've done every part of it yourself, you have a much better sense of what you're asking people to do, how long things really take, and how to help when someone's stuck. That's been really important for me in building teams and at Arc, because we're trying to do ambitious, long-horizon science, and you need people who understand the whole arc of a project, not just their slice of it.

And honestly, there's a confidence that comes from it. Once you've shipped something complete, even something small, you know you can do it again. That compounds. You start taking on bigger and harder problems because you've internalized that the messy middle is survivable.

r001.rationale: The response describes benefits of taking projects end to end, but does not say that fewer people complete whole projects than complete intermediate steps.

r002.rationale: It mentions bottlenecks and the messy middle, but gives no 20%/80% estimate.

r003.rationale: It says completing something builds confidence that you can do it again, but does not state that repeatedly finishing projects hones an instinct for bringing work to completion.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think there's something that happens when you actually take an idea all the way through to the end that you just can't get from doing pieces of things. When I was a grad student, the thing I was most grateful for was that I got to own a project from the very first question all the way to the paper being published and the tools being out in the world. And that process teaches you things that no amount of reading or watching other people do it can teach you.

Part of it is that you learn where the real difficulty is. At the start, you have this model in your head of what's going to be hard, and it's almost always wrong. The thing you thought would take two weeks takes eight months, and the thing you were terrified of turns out to be trivial. You only learn that calibration by going through the whole arc. And once you've done it once, you have this intuition for the shape of a project that makes you much better at planning the next one, and at knowing when something is actually stuck versus just uncomfortable.

The other thing is confidence, honestly. Science is mostly failure. Most experiments don't work. And if you've never seen something through to completion, it's really hard to tell yourself in month six of nothing working that it's going to be okay. But if you've done it before, you have this reference point. You know what it feels like when things are actually converging versus when they're not. So I think about it as building a kind of internal compass. And I try to give the people in my lab that same experience, because I think it changes who you are as a scientist.

r001.rationale: The response says owning a project end to end teaches skills that doing isolated pieces cannot, but it does not say this distinguishes a smaller group of people.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the final 20% taking roughly 80% of the work.

r003.rationale: The response says completing a project once improves planning and helps calibrate whether work is stuck, but it does not state that repeatedly finishing projects hones an instinct for bringing work to completion.

astra-6.text:
I think you learn something fundamentally different from finishing a project than you do from starting one. At the beginning, you have an idea and a sense of how it might work. Then you encounter all the details you didn’t anticipate, and you have to decide what to change, what to let go of, and what’s essential to the original goal.

Going through that whole cycle gives you better judgment the next time. You can work backward from an outcome and understand what it actually takes to get there. And it builds a kind of confidence grounded in experience: you’ve been stuck before, you’ve figured things out, and you’ve brought something across the finish line.

r001.rationale: It describes the different learning from finishing a project, but does not say that finishing distinguishes a smaller group of people than completing intermediate steps.

r002.rationale: It does not mention the final 20% or that it accounts for roughly 80% of the work.

r003.rationale: It says the experience improves judgment and builds confidence, but does not clearly state that repeatedly finishing projects hones an instinct for bringing work to completion.

sol-6.1.text:
Because there’s a huge difference between having an idea and making it work. When you take a project all the way through, you encounter the details you couldn’t have anticipated at the beginning. You have to troubleshoot, make tradeoffs, and decide what’s actually essential. That’s where a lot of the learning happens.

And it gives you a different kind of confidence. The next time you face an ambiguous problem, you have some experience turning uncertainty into a finished result. So I value that experience more than just having been involved in a lot of projects.

r001.rationale: It contrasts finishing a project with merely having an idea or being involved in projects, but does not say that finishing distinguishes a smaller group of people than completing intermediate steps.

r002.rationale: It mentions unforeseen details and troubleshooting, but gives no 20%/80% estimate or equivalent claim about the final portion accounting for most of the work.

r003.rationale: It says finishing provides experience and confidence, but does not state that repeatedly finishing projects hones an instinct for completion.
